questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Total Area Bounded Between the X-Axis and a Curve
questions.problem: Find the total area of the region between the curve $y=4{x}^{3}+4$ and the $x$-axis from $x=-2$ to $x=1.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the intersections of the curve with the $x$-axis:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{3}+4 & =0 \\ {x}^{3} & =-1 \\ x & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x=-1$ is our only real solution. Since $-1\in [-2,1]$, we have two regions: 

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=-2$ to $x=-1.$

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=-1$ to $x=1.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14030836/assets/b0f2899bf6a946f6d7bf8bc60c41827bd05aef500f0fc0f30a5916c26b1007bb.png)

Notice that the region for $x\in [-2,-1]$ lies completely below the $x$-axis. Hence, the value of

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-2}^{-1}(4{x}^{3}+4)\,\text{d}x
$$

will be negative. Therefore, the area that we want is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1} & =-{\int }_{-2}^{-1}(4{x}^{3}+4)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-4{\int }_{-2}^{-1}{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x-4{\int }_{-2}^{-1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{x}^{4}{|}_{-2}^{-1}-4x{|}_{-2}^{-1} \\  & =-[(-1)^{4}-(-2)^{4}]-4[-1+2] \\  & =-(-15)-4 \\  & =11.\end{aligned}
$$

For $x\in [-1,1]$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{2} & ={\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(4{x}^{3}+4)\,\text{d}x \\  & =4{\int }_{-1}^{1}{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x+4{\int }_{-1}^{1}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={x}^{4}{|}_{-1}^{1}+4x{|}_{-1}^{-1} \\  & =[{1}^{4}-(-1)^{4}]+4[1-(-1)] \\  & =0+8 \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the total area is

$$
A={A}_{1}+{A}_{2}=11+8=19.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Total Area Bounded By a Curve When It Crosses the X-Axis Several Times
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14030836/assets/a8a85024d555378ad7ba31262a290386777fa94b00208d6a68fdacb5bb61d3c8.png)

Which integral expression gives the total area enclosed between the curve $y={x}^{3}-x$ and the $x$-axis, as shown above?
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the limits of integration. We find the $x$-intercepts of the curve as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}-x & =0 \\ x({x}^{2}-1) & =0 \\ x(x-1)(x+1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So we have $x=\pm 1$ or $x=0.$ Since $0\in [-1,1],$ we have two regions: 

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=-1$ to $x=0.$

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=0$ to $x=1.$

For $x\in [-1,0]$, we have

$$
{A}_{1}={\int }_{-1}^{0}({x}^{3}-x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Notice that for $x\in [0,1]$ the region lies completely below the $x$-axis. Hence, the value of

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-1}^{0}({x}^{3}-x)\,\text{d}x
$$

will be negative. Therefore, the area that we want is given by

$$
{A}_{2}=-{\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{3}-x)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{0}^{1}-({x}^{3}-x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Finally, the total area is

$$
A={A}_{1}+{A}_{2}={\int }_{-1}^{0}({x}^{3}-x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{1}-({x}^{3}-x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Total Area Bounded Between the X-Axis and a Curve
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14030836/assets/47e15993f3957fb3c1d7619fcf62544b2d5b358715538e17b9232dec5a0172c7.png)

Find the total area of the region between the curve $y={x}^{4}-1$ and the $x$-axis from $x=0$ to $x=2$, as shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the intersections of the curve with the $x$-axis:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{4}-1 & =0 \\ {x}^{4} & =1 \\ x & =\pm 1.\end{aligned}
$$

The only solution between $x=0$ and $x=2$ is $x=1.$

Since $1\in [0,2]$, we have two regions: 

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=0$ to $x=1.$

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=1$ to $x=2.$

Notice that the region for $x\in [0,1]$ lies completely below the $x$-axis. Hence, the value of

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{4}-1)\,\text{d}x
$$

will be negative. Therefore, the area that we want is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1} & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{4}-1)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{(\frac{{x}^{5}}{5}-x)|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-[\frac{1}{5}-1]-0 \\  & =\frac{4}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

For $x\in [1,2]$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{2} & ={\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}({x}^{4}-1)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(\frac{{x}^{5}}{5}-x)|}_{1}^{2} \\  & =([\frac{32}{5}-2]-[\frac{1}{5}-1]) \\  & =\frac{26}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the total area is

$$
A={A}_{1}+{A}_{2}=\frac{4}{5}+\frac{26}{5}=\frac{30}{5}=6.
$$

questions.problem: Find the total area of the region between the curve $y=3x+3{x}^{2}$ and the $x$-axis from $x=-2$ to $x=0.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the intersections of the curve with the $x$-axis:

$$
\begin{aligned}3x+3{x}^{2} & =0 \\ 3x(1+x) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x=-1$ and $x=0$ are our real solutions. Since $-1\in [-2,0]$, we have two regions: 

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=-2$ to $x=-1.$

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=-1$ to $x=0.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14030836/assets/16a25fdc08ed6db39932508fd829dc5f855b38ff9ec85083a08d05fed0d985ab.png)

For $x\in [-2,-1]$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1} & ={\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{-1}(3x+3{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{\int }_{-2}^{-1}x\,\text{d}x+3{\int }_{-2}^{-1}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}{|}_{-2}^{-1}+{x}^{3}{|}_{-2}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}[(-1)^{2}-(-2)^{2}]+[(-1)^{3}-(-2)^{3}] \\  & =-\frac{9}{2}+7 \\  & =\frac{5}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that for $x\in [-1,0]$ the region lies completely below the $x$-axis. Hence, the value of

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-1}^{0}(3x+3{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x
$$

will be negative. Therefore, the area that we want is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{2} & =-{\int }_{-1}^{0}(3x+3{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =-3{\int }_{-1}^{0}x\,\text{d}x-3{\int }_{-1}^{0}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}{|}_{-1}^{0}-{x}^{3}{|}_{-1}^{0} \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}[0-(-1)^{2}]-[0-(-1)^{3}] \\  & =\frac{3}{2}-1 \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the total area is

$$
A={A}_{1}+{A}_{2}=\frac{5}{2}+\frac{1}{2}=3.
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14030836/assets/27bb4ee622f0b80e4b1a6edfae2c42f0676cafd0f9ad6150b979b32dbdabfc62.png)

Which integral expression gives the total area enclosed between the curve $y=4{x}^{3}-{x}^{5}$ and the $x$-axis, as shown above?
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the limits of integration. We find the $x$-intercepts of the curve as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{3}-{x}^{5} & =0 \\ {x}^{3}(4-{x}^{2}) & =0 \\ {x}^{3}(2-x)(2+x) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So we have $x=\pm 2$ or $x=0.$ Since $0\in [-2,2],$ we have two regions: 

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=-2$ to $x=0.$

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=0$ to $x=2.$

Notice that for $x\in [-2,0]$ the region lies completely below the $x$-axis. Hence, the value of

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-2}^{0}(4{x}^{3}-{x}^{5})\,\text{d}x
$$

will be negative. Therefore, the area that we want is given by

$$
{A}_{1}=-{\int }_{-2}^{0}(4{x}^{3}-{x}^{5})\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-2}^{0}-(4{x}^{3}-{x}^{5})\,\text{d}x.
$$

For $x\in [0,2]$, we have

$$
{A}_{2}={\int }_{0}^{2}(4{x}^{3}-{x}^{5})\,\text{d}x.
$$

Finally, the total area is

$$
A={A}_{1}+{A}_{2}={\int }_{-2}^{0}-(4{x}^{3}-{x}^{5})\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{2}(4{x}^{3}-{x}^{5})\,\text{d}x.
$$
